name: Platforms serving two sides
idea: An encyclopedia article states that a two-sided market is a platform between two distinct user groups that give each other network benefits; when one group cares how many users the other has, that is a cross-side network effect. It reports a rule found in one firm's case: subsidise the more price-sensitive side and charge the side whose demand grows more as the other side grows.
suggests: Look at whether a company brings together two groups that value each other, which side it charges and which it subsidises, and how many users each side already has.
limits: The article states that network effects alone, cross-side or same-side, do not make a firm a multi-sided platform. It adds that the end value of two-sided pricing depends on the market and may not cover its costs, and that a platform should take more care when the product it gives away has appreciable unit costs.
competing_idea: Another view the article sets out and argues against: pricing each side without regard to network effects, seeking the biggest revenue under each side's demand curve. The article states that in two-sided networks such logic can be misguided, since adoption on one side drives adoption on the other.
questions: Which two groups does the platform bring together, and how much does each value the size of the other?
Which side pays and which side is subsidised, and does the subsidised side respond more to price?
Does the company's pricing take account of how growth on one side raises demand on the other?

originals.reference: "Two-sided market", Wikipedia, The Free Encyclopedia, revision 1385019671 of 11 November 2026
originals.about: Jean-Charles Rochet and Jean Tirole, "Platform Competition in Two-Sided Markets", Journal of the European Economic Association, Vol. 1 No. 4, 2003, pp. 990-1029; Thomas Eisenmann, Geoffrey G. Parker and Marshall W. Van Alstyne, "Strategies for Two-Sided Markets", Harvard Business Review, October 2006
